title: FCC plans robocall scorecard to grade phone companies on spam call blocking
gist: The FCC proposed a public robocall-mitigation scorecard grading wireless, wireline, and VoIP providers on both process compliance and measurable outcomes in blocking illegal robocalls, seeking public comment on data sources amid skepticism from consumer advocates about data quality and provider self-reporting bias.

insights.claim: The FCC's proposed robocall scorecard would rate domestic wireless, wireline, and VoIP providers with retail customers (excluding wholesale/intermediate-only providers) using either a number scale, letter grades, or low/medium/high risk classifications, based on call-blocking statistics, customer complaints, and enforcement actions.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A public grading system directly affects telecom carrier reputations and could become a consumer-facing competitive differentiator or liability, similar to existing FCC broadband labels — relevant for telecom sector investors tracking regulatory/reputational risk.
insights.locator: The scorecards could include call-blocking statistics

insights.claim: The FCC explicitly wants to move beyond a simple administrative compliance checklist toward a composite set of metrics reflecting both operational practices and measurable outcomes, including how often legitimate calls are erroneously blocked.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Including false-positive (over-blocking legitimate calls) metrics adds a two-sided accountability standard for carriers, meaning providers can be penalized for both under- and over-blocking — a more complex compliance bar for telecom operators.
insights.quote: moving beyond a simple administrative checklist (i.e., did the provider file the right paperwork, did they offer the right tools) and toward a composite set of metrics that reflects both operational practices and measurable outcomes, including how often legitimate calls are blocked

insights.claim: Proposed data sources for the scorecard include consumer complaints filed with the FCC and FTC, FCC enforcement actions, filings with the Robocall Mitigation Database (where providers certify STIR/SHAKEN Caller ID verification implementation), and data from the Industry Traceback Group, a telecom industry group that traces illegal robocall sources.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Names the specific existing regulatory data infrastructure (STIR/SHAKEN filings, Traceback Group) the scorecard will likely draw on, giving a concrete sense of what data becomes newly public and how carriers might be scored.
insights.locator: Other proposed sources of data include FCC enforcement actions

themes.theme: Consumer advocate skepticism and data-quality concerns

insights.claim: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr called combatting illegal robocalls the FCC's top consumer protection priority and said the scorecard will give consumers more information while incentivizing providers to improve efforts.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Signals this is a stated top FCC priority under Chairman Carr, suggesting continued regulatory attention and likely follow-through toward finalizing the scorecard rule.
insights.quote: Combatting the scourge of illegal robocalls remains the FCC's top consumer protection priority

insights.claim: Teresa Murray of PIRG, who previously authored a February 2025 report grading providers on robocall blocking, said the FCC's robocall efforts 'have been disappointing for years' and expressed concern about what information the FCC will actually use and whether it will be useful to consumers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A consumer advocate with direct prior experience grading providers is skeptical of the FCC's execution, an important counterweight to the FCC's own framing and a signal the scorecard's ultimate usefulness is uncertain.
insights.quote: The FCC's efforts have been disappointing for years, going back to even before Congress passed the robocall crackdown law in 2019
insights.locator: "We applaud the FCC's possible renewed interest"

insights.claim: The FCC itself raised the question of whether providers are a reliable or even the only source of scorecard data, and whether third-party data sources such as call analytics companies are unbiased or have incentives to skew results in favor of certain providers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The FCC's own acknowledgment of potential data-source bias (including reliance on self-reported provider data) is a credibility risk for the scorecard's eventual usefulness and a key item to watch in the final rule.
insights.quote: Are such data sources unbiased, i.e., do not have an interest in skewing results in favor of certain providers?
insights.locator: Are there other parties that might have helpful data

insights.claim: Murray argued that switching phone or VoIP providers is not as easy as switching grocery stores, even for customers not under contract, implying that a scorecard's practical power to drive consumer switching behavior may be limited despite its potential to 'shame' providers into improving.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Highlights a structural limit on market-based accountability mechanisms in telecom: even with transparency, switching friction constrains competitive discipline, meaning the scorecard's main effect may be reputational/shaming rather than direct market-share shifts.
insights.quote: switching cellphone or VoIP providers isn't as easy as choosing to shop at a different grocery store next week, even if someone isn't in a phone contract

insights.claim: Carr previously led an FCC vote to stop requiring that ISPs list all their discretionary fees on the FCC's existing broadband pricing labels, cited as prior context for how the FCC's consumer-transparency initiatives can be later scaled back.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A precedent of the same chairman rolling back a related transparency requirement (broadband fee disclosure) is a relevant signal for judging how durable or robust the new robocall scorecard's requirements might end up being.
insights.locator: though Carr recently led a vote to stop requiring
